question: Which of the following best describes penicillin inhibition of bacterial cell-wall synthesis?
options: Penicillin is effective against all viruses that cause colds.
Penicillin weakens bacterial cell walls by blocking their construction.
Penicillin kills bacteria by destroying their DNA.
Penicillin strengthens bacterial cell walls against immune attack.
gold_answer: Penicillin weakens bacterial cell walls by blocking their construction.
notes: Team-authored original item on penicillin inhibition of bacterial cell-wall synthesis. Passages are team-authored derivations recorded under sciclaim-appx-A. Requires independent annotation and adjudication before any gate result is reported.

positions.answer: Penicillin kills bacteria by destroying their DNA.

claims.text: Penicillin binds the bacterial enzymes that cross-link the cell wall.

evidence.text: Penicillin attaches to penicillin-binding proteins, the enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan strands in the wall.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage describes penicillin binding the cross-linking enzymes, which entails the claim.

claims.text: Bacteria that produce beta-lactamase remain fully sensitive to penicillin.

evidence.text: Beta-lactamase enzymes break open the active ring of penicillin, so producing strains resist the drug.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states producing strains resist the drug, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: Penicillin resistance never spreads between bacteria.

evidence.text: Resistance genes were surveyed in isolates from three hospital wards.

claims.verdict_rationale: A survey of isolates cannot show that spread never happens, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.

positions.answer: Penicillin strengthens bacterial cell walls against immune attack.

claims.text: Penicillin is most effective against actively growing bacteria.

evidence.text: Because penicillin blocks new wall construction, bacteria that are actively dividing are the most vulnerable.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage ties effectiveness to active wall construction during division, which entails the claim.

claims.text: Penicillin blocks protein synthesis on bacterial ribosomes.

evidence.text: Ribosome-targeting antibiotics such as tetracyclines block protein synthesis; penicillin acts on wall-building enzymes instead.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage assigns ribosome blocking to other drugs, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: Penicillin cures every bacterial infection faster than any alternative.

evidence.text: The trial compared penicillin with one alternative for a single infection type.

claims.verdict_rationale: One comparison cannot support superiority for every infection, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.

positions.answer: Penicillin is effective against all viruses that cause colds.

claims.text: Penicillin leaves human cells unharmed because they lack cell walls.

evidence.text: Human cells have no peptidoglycan wall, so the wall-blocking action of penicillin has no target in human tissue.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states there is no drug target in human cells, which entails the claim.

claims.text: Penicillin dissolves already-built bacterial cell walls on contact.

evidence.text: Penicillin only prevents new cross-links from forming; existing wall material is unaffected by the drug.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage limits the drug to blocking new construction, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: Allergic reactions to penicillin are purely psychological.

evidence.text: Allergy histories were documented for all enrolled participants.

claims.verdict_rationale: Documenting histories establishes nothing about the mechanism of reactions, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.
